title: DHS Is Hiring Bounty Hunters to Find and Photograph Deported People’s Homes Abroad
gist: CBP is soliciting private investigators to locate and photograph the foreign homes of deported immigrants under a $9 million, two-year 'Tracing and Payment Recovery Services' contract covering Mexico, Honduras and Guatemala, extending a domestic skip-tracing bounty-hunter model (already worth up to $1.2 billion via ICE contracts) to people who have already left the US.

themes.theme: New government contracting opportunity: overseas skip-tracing

insights.claim: US Customs and Border Protection documents cap a new 'Tracing and Payment Recovery Services' program at $9 million over the next two years, seeking private investigators to confirm the home addresses of deported immigrants in Mexico, Honduras, and Guatemala, and potentially other countries, using commercial data verification and physical observation including photographs of the home.
insights.speaker: Dell Cameron
insights.so_what: A concrete, bid-out federal contract ($9M cap, bids due August 7) creates a new commercial niche for private investigation and skip-tracing firms; investors tracking govtech/security-services contractors should watch for which vendors win this and the ICE program below.
insights.locator: The documents, which cap the so-called Tracing and Payment Recovery Services program

insights.claim: CBP's overseas program extends a model it already runs domestically: in December, Immigration and Customs Enforcement awarded open-ended skip-tracing contracts to 13 private companies potentially worth a combined $1.2 billion over two years, with contractors earning bonuses based on the number of people found.
insights.speaker: Dell Cameron
insights.so_what: $1.2 billion committed to domestic skip-tracing contractors (per Scripps News reporting cited) shows the scale of the private-sector immigration-enforcement data industry already in place, of which the new $9M overseas program is an incremental extension — a fast-growing, policy-driven revenue stream for data-broker and PI firms.
insights.locator: CBP's proposal extends a model the government has already built

insights.claim: Contractors under the program would be paid a set fee per person documented, with tiered bonuses for reporting back within 7, 14, or 28 days, and payment is not contingent on any money actually being recovered from the deportee; the government would retain unlimited ownership and reuse rights over all data investigators gather.
insights.speaker: Dell Cameron
insights.so_what: The incentive structure rewards speed and volume of address-finding over successful debt collection, and government retention of unlimited data rights means any commercial or public data aggregated by contractors becomes a permanent, reusable government asset — relevant to data-privacy and civil-liberties risk assessments for firms bidding on the contract.
insights.locator: Contractors hired under the Tracing and Payment Recovery Services program

themes.theme: Scale and mechanics of the underlying fine regime

insights.claim: As of July, DHS says it has issued more than $84 billion in fines to immigrants accused of failing to depart the US, citing an obscure provision of a 1996 immigration law that went unused until Donald Trump's first term; fines run at $998 a day for up to five years and some individual fines have reached $1.8 million.
insights.speaker: Dell Cameron
insights.so_what: An $84 billion nominal liability pool, even if largely uncollectible, represents a huge pipeline for third-party debt collectors and now overseas tracing contractors — a policy-driven market size figure worth tracking for exposure to affected sectors (debt collection, legal services).
insights.locator: As of July, the Department of Homeland Security

insights.claim: The three debt collection agencies CBP already uses had, as of July, not located a single person outside the US, even though the government estimates it has removed about 66,387 people who are carrying unpaid CBP fines and penalties.
insights.speaker: Dell Cameron
insights.so_what: A near-total collection failure rate (zero located out of tens of thousands of cases) is the direct rationale CBP cites for the new physical-tracing contract — signals the government sees this as an unmet market need rather than a redundant program.
insights.locator: The three debt collection agencies CBP already uses

insights.claim: DHS promises to forgive failure-to-depart fines for people who self-deport via the CBP Home app, but this waiver excludes a separate $5,130 fee that Congress created for people ordered removed in absentia and later arrested by ICE, a fee the statute explicitly bars from being waived or reduced.
insights.speaker: Dell Cameron
insights.so_what: A carve-out fee immune to the standard forgiveness pathway means self-deportation does not guarantee a clean slate, undermining the government's own incentive program and creating latent legal/compliance risk for anyone relying on the waiver.
insights.locator: DHS promises that it will forgive failure-to-depart fines

insights.claim: Legal Aid Society immigration attorney Hasan Shafiqullah says he has seen some third-party collection agencies add up to $500,000 in additional administrative fees on top of the government's original fine amounts.
insights.speaker: Hasan Shafiqullah (via Dell Cameron)
insights.so_what: Private collection agencies operating in this space are adding substantial markup fees, indicating the private-collections layer of this program may be more lucrative (and more legally contestable) than the underlying government fines themselves.
insights.locator: Hasan Shafiqullah, the Legal Aid Society's immigration supervising attorney

insights.claim: NYU law professor Alina Das, director of the school's Immigrant Rights Clinic, characterizes pursuing overseas fine collection against people who have already left the country as a 'significant escalation in tactics.'
insights.speaker: Alina Das (via Dell Cameron)
insights.so_what: Legal experts frame this program as a notable policy escalation, which raises the likelihood of litigation or legislative pushback that could affect contract continuity or scope for firms bidding on it.
insights.locator: Alina Das, a law professor and director of NYU's Immigrant Rights Clinic

insights.claim: Senators Dick Durbin and Alex Padilla wrote to the acting attorney general and DHS secretary in July asking them to stop applying the fines to immigrants complying with the law and to disclose how many penalties went to people with pending/lawful status or to survivors of domestic violence and trafficking; as of publication, neither department had responded to the senators' July 31 deadline.
insights.speaker: Dell Cameron
insights.so_what: Congressional oversight requests going unanswered signals limited near-term legislative check on the program, suggesting the contract is likely to proceed on schedule despite political criticism.
insights.locator: Senators Dick Durbin and Alex Padilla wrote to acting attorney general

insights.claim: CBP's solicitation does not specify where contractors' commercial data on deportees would come from, only requiring contractors to disclose their skip-tracing methods, tools, and resources after work is already underway.
insights.speaker: Dell Cameron
insights.so_what: The lack of upfront data-sourcing requirements creates ambiguity around use of foreign public records versus commercial credit data, a compliance and reputational risk factor for any contractor and their data suppliers.
insights.locator: The documents say contractors would use commercial data
